In contrast, Franklin D. Roosevelt believed the federal government needed to play a much larger role in the economy. For example, he proposed national policy changes to increase crop prices so that farming could be more profitable. He also talked about giving direct aid to people who had lost their jobs. He promised a "New Deal" for Americans, saying, "Every man has a right to life; and this means that he has also a right to make a comfortable living." Such ideas appealed to Americans who worked long hours for little pay.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt, also known as FDR, ran against Herbert Hoover in the 1932 presidential election. Read the passage about Hoover and Roosevelt. Then follow the directions below.

mainText.text: President Herbert Hoover believed the Great Depression needed to be solved by private businesses. He consulted with business leaders about how to respond to the economic crisis and often listened to their suggestions. He also gave loans to major companies like investment banks and railroads. Hoover avoided strict business regulations or giving citizens direct aid. He believed those approaches would give the federal government too much control over the economy.

In contrast, Franklin D. Roosevelt believed the federal government needed to play a much larger role in the economy. For example, he proposed national policy changes to increase crop prices so that farming could be more profitable. He also talked about giving direct aid to people who had lost their jobs. He promised a "New Deal" for Americans, saying, "Every man has a right to life; and this means that he has also a right to make a comfortable living." Such ideas appealed to Americans who worked long hours for little pay.

contents.text: Franklin D. Roosevelt, also known as FDR, ran against Herbert Hoover in the 1932 presidential election. Read the passage about Hoover and Roosevelt. Then follow the directions below.

mainText.text: President Herbert Hoover believed the Great Depression needed to be solved by private businesses. He consulted with business leaders about how to respond to the economic crisis and often listened to their suggestions. He also gave loans to major companies like investment banks and railroads. Hoover avoided strict business regulations or giving citizens direct aid. He believed those approaches would give the federal government too much control over the economy.

In contrast, Franklin D. Roosevelt believed the federal government needed to play a much larger role in the economy. For example, he proposed national policy changes to increase crop prices so that farming could be more profitable. He also talked about giving direct aid to people who had lost their jobs. He promised a "New Deal" for Americans, saying, "Every man has a right to life; and this means that he has also a right to make a comfortable living." Such ideas appealed to Americans who worked long hours for little pay.

table.text: Many people had invested money in the stock market. But in 1929, stock values fell dramatically.

pieces.text: Investors make money when their stock values increase. If their stocks lose value, investors lose money. So,

content.text: people lost billions of dollars when their shares of stock became practically worthless

pieces.text: after the stock market crash.

table.text: After the stock market crash, many people panicked and withdrew their money from banks at the same time.

pieces.text: Since bank customers took out all their money at the same time,

content.text: many banks did not have enough cash and had to permanently close, wiping out customers' savings

table.text: After 1929, people had less money to spend, and businesses struggled to sell products.

pieces.text: Since businesses couldn't sell products, they had a hard time making money. So,

content.text: faced with a sharp decline in sales, many companies cut costs by firing workers, leading to widespread unemployment
